title: Is the table real? The two truths
carry: two truths: it works, yet doesn't stand alone
tomorrow: point to your body. where exactly is it?

cards: Knock on a table. Solid. It holds your coffee, your laptop, your elbows at dinner.
Now take away the legs, the top, the screws, the wood, and the word table we all agreed on. What's left over? Nothing.
It's an odd question to ask about furniture. It's also a real one. So is the table real or not?
Shantideva's answer: yes, and it depends which truth you're asking.

teach.b: He says there are two truths: the conventional and the ultimate. Conventional truth is the world as it works. Tables hold cups, names call people, kindness helps.

teach.h: BEYOND THE REACH OF THE INTELLECT.
teach.b: Ultimate truth is how things are when you look all the way down, and there he says something startling: the ultimate is not within reach of the intellect, because the intellect itself belongs to the conventional.
Neither truth cancels the other. The table really holds your cup. And it isn't a thing standing on its own apart from its parts and our naming.
A neighbor tradition says something close.

teach.h: THE TAO THAT CAN BE TRODDEN.
teach.b: The old Chinese book of the Tao, in James Legge's English: "The Tao that can be trodden is not the enduring and unchanging Tao." Shared ground: words and ideas reach only so far; what's deepest is beyond what we can name.
One honest difference. The book speaks of the nameless Tao as the origin of heaven and earth, a source. Shantideva's ultimate isn't a source things come from; it's that nothing stands on its own.
Two maps of the edge of words.

how: The two truths are a central teaching in Mahayana philosophy, studied in debate and commentary; many Buddhist teachers use everyday objects, like a chariot or a table, to show both views.

o: the everyday view and the deepest view of things
a polite truth and the harsh truth behind it
two rival schools that each claim to be right

games.q: a friend who loves the Tao Te Ching says, 'so Shantideva and Laozi teach the same thing.' what's a fair reply?
o: both say words fall short of what's deepest; the Tao is a source, Shantideva's ultimate isn't.
yes, identical; they only used different languages.
no, nothing in common; one book is Chinese and one is Indian.
games.why: shared ground: the edge of words. honest difference: the book calls the nameless Tao the origin of heaven and earth; Shantideva's ultimate is no source at all.

practice: Pick up or look at one ordinary thing near you: a mug, a pen, your phone. First describe it the everyday way, in a sentence: what it is and what it's for.
Then look again and name its parts one by one, and notice there's no extra piece called mug among them. Hold both views at once.

wordCard.voice: Two truths: the conventional and the ultimate. Things work as they seem, and they aren't what they seem.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the conventional, the everyday level of truth.

carryVoice: The line to hold: two truths: it works, yet doesn't stand alone. The cup holds coffee, and doesn't stand on its own. Forty-two days into the guide.

sources.ref: Bodhicaryavatara 9.2 (the conventional and the ultimate: these are the two truths; the ultimate is not within reach of the intellect)
